entry.title: Token Budgeting
entry.summary: Modern generative AI applications offer unprecedented capabilities, yet their operational costs can quickly escalate. The primary driver of these costs, alongside computational resources, is token consumption. Understanding and implementing effective token budgeting strategies is not merely an optimization; it is fundamental to building scalable, efficient, and economically viable AI systems. Tokens are the atomic units of text that large language models (LLMs) process. Whether you're sending a prompt (input tokens) or receiving a response (output tokens), each token incurs a cost. This cost varies by model, but the principle remains: more tokens mean higher expenses and often, increased latency due to longer processing times. entry.summary:
0 % vs 50 %: making a RAG agent refuse to hallucinate
2026-05-31 · LLM / RAG A retrieval-augmented agent is only as trustworthy as its behaviour on questions whose answer isn't in the corpus. The failure mode is quiet: instead of saying "I don't know," the model measures it. Reference architecture: nim-agent-blueprint — agentic RAG on The agent loop is plan → retrieve → generate → validate. The interesting variable is the
Configuration Out-of-corpus hallucination rate
Generate freely from context ~50 %
Guarded prompt (answer only from context; otherwise abstain) 0 %
Same model, same retriever, same questions. The only change is a prompt that makes "I can't validate recall@3 stayed at 94–100 %, so the guardrail buys safety without The lesson isn't the prompt — it's that the difference between 50 % and 0 % is invisible . A demo that only asks in-corpus questions looks perfect in both score groundedness. So the blueprint ships with: retrieval hit-rate (is the answer even retrievable?), answer groundedness via LLM-as-judge (is the answer supported by what was retrieved?), latency, and OpenTelemetry traces per agent step. That's the difference between "it works on my five questions" and "here is the number a For enterprise RAG, abstention is a feature, not a failure. Google just redesigned the search box for the first time in 25 years — here’s why it matters more than you think.
entry.summary: For a quarter century, the Google search box has been one of the most recognizable interfaces in computing: a thin white rectangle, a blinking cursor, a few typed words, and a list of blue links.
